title: From recursion to a table
sub: Climbing Stairs and Unique Paths: memoization, a table, two variables — and the five questions any DP is built from
cards/0/title: Climbing Stairs and the signals of DP
cards/0/body:
Climbing Stairs (LeetCode #70). A staircase of n steps, 1 ≤ n ≤ 45. Each move climbs 1 or 2 steps. In how many ways can you reach the top? For n = 3 — three: 1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1.

The signals of dynamic programming (DP):

1. The question asks for a number of ways, a minimum/maximum, or “is it possible” — not a list of options.
2. The answer is built from answers to the same problem of a smaller size: the last move was either 1 or 2, so the ways to reach n are the ways to reach n − 1 plus the ways to reach n − 2.
3. These smaller problems repeat — they are reached along different paths.

The first two points give a recursion, and it is correct. The third says that the recursion does the same work many times — and that is what DP cures.
cards/0/code:
// straight from the definition: correct, but exponential
int Climb(int n) => n <= 1 ? 1 : Climb(n - 1) + Climb(n - 2);
cards/1/q: How many calls does Climb(45) from the previous card make, and what follows from that?
cards/1/options/0: ≈ 3.7·10⁹ — tens of seconds, it won’t fit the limit
cards/1/options/1: ≈ 45 — one call per step, it’s instant
cards/1/explain: The number of calls is C(n) = 1 + C(n − 1) + C(n − 2) — it grows like the answer itself, about 1.618 times per step. Climb(45) = 1 836 311 903, and there are almost twice as many calls: 3 672 623 805. At the rule of thumb of 10⁸ operations per second, that is more than 30 seconds.
cards/1/wrong/1: One call per step would be the case if every step were computed once. Here Climb(43) is called from both Climb(45) and Climb(44) — and so on at every level.
cards/1/wrong/2: The number of calls grows not like a square but exponentially: every call spawns two. The answer for n = 45 is almost two billion ways, and there are even more calls.
cards/2/body:
Draw the call tree for n = 5: Climb(3) appears twice, Climb(2) three times, Climb(1) five times. There are only n + 1 distinct subproblems — 0 to n — but exponentially many calls: the same thing is computed again and again. That is signal 3 — overlapping subproblems.

Memoization means remembering a subproblem’s answer the first time it is computed and returning it on every repeated call. The code stays a top-down recursion, but each step is computed once: O(n) time, O(n) memory for the array and O(n) for the call stack.

The array needs a “not computed yet” mark. Here 0 works: no step has zero ways. If 0 is a legitimate answer, use -1 or int?[]. If the states are sparse and large (a pair of coordinates, a string), use a Dictionary.
cards/3/title: A bottom-up table and the five questions of DP
cards/3/body:
Memoization computes subproblems in whatever order the recursion reaches them. If the order is known in advance — from small to large — the recursion is not needed: we fill a table with a loop. No stack, no “computed yet?” checks, and you can see which cells are needed.

Every DP is assembled from five answers, worth saying out loud before the code:

1. State — what a cell means: ways[i] is the number of ways to reach step i.
2. Transition — how a cell is expressed through smaller ones: ways[i] = ways[i − 1] + ways[i − 2].
3. Base — cells not derived by the transition: ways[0] = ways[1] = 1.
4. Order — everything the transition refers to is computed earlier: i ascending.
5. Answer — where it lies: ways[n].

And then — memory: the transition only looks at the two previous values, so two variables are enough. O(n) time, O(1) memory.
cards/4/q: Build the table version of Climbing Stairs.
cards/4/explain: The answer lies in ways[n], so there are n + 1 cells. The base: one way to stand on the ground and one way to reach the first step. The loop includes n: with i < n, ways[n] would stay zero. The transition is the last move of 1 or 2.
cards/5/task: Walk the table filling for n = 6. The rig will stop twice and ask what goes into a cell and what the code actually needed.
cards/5/goal/asks/0/q: ways[2] = 2, ways[3] = 3. What goes into ways[4]?
cards/5/goal/asks/0/explain: Step 4 is reached from the third with a move of 1 or from the second with a move of 2: 3 + 2 = 5. 4 is “one way per step”, 6 is doubling ways[3]: that would happen if both moves led from every step to the same place.
cards/5/goal/asks/1/q: ways[6] = 8 + 5 = 13. Which cells did the code read on the last step?
cards/5/goal/asks/1/explain: The transition looks at exactly the two previous cells. Everything further left will never be needed again — that is why the table folds into two variables prev and cur: O(n) time, O(1) memory.
cards/6/q: The two-variable version returns 4 instead of 3 for n = 3. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/6/explain: prev = cur overwrites the old prev before it is used: after that cur = cur + cur, and the values just double — 1, 2, 4. The window has to slide at once: (prev, cur) = (cur, prev + cur), or with a temporary int next = prev + cur; prev = cur; cur = next.
cards/7/title: Unique Paths: the same idea on a grid
cards/7/body:
Unique Paths (LeetCode #62). A robot stands in the top-left corner of an m × n grid (up to 100 × 100) and moves only right or down. How many paths lead to the bottom-right corner? The answer is guaranteed to be at most 2·10⁹.

The five questions. State: dp[r, c] is the number of paths to cell (r, c). Transition: a cell is entered from above or from the left — dp[r − 1, c] + dp[r, c − 1]. Base: the top row and the left column have one path each. Order: rows top to bottom, left to right within a row. Answer: dp[m − 1, n − 1]. Time and memory O(m·n). For 3 × 7 the answer is 28.

O(n) memory. A row only needs the previous row, and even that doesn’t have to be stored separately: in a one-dimensional row, before the update row[c] still holds the value from above, and row[c − 1] already holds the new one from the left. So row[c] += row[c − 1].

Combinatorics. Every path is m − 1 moves down and n − 1 moves right in some order, so the answer is C(m + n − 2, m − 1). It is computed in O(min(m, n)) with long. But the formula breaks under any change of the problem: obstacles (Unique Paths II, #63 — dp = 0 in a rock cell), cell costs (Minimum Path Sum, #64 — grid[r, c] + min(above, left)). The table survives all of them.
cards/8/q: Build Unique Paths with O(n) memory.
cards/8/explain: The top row has one path into each cell, hence Fill(row, 1). The left column is always 1 too, so c starts at 1 and row[0] is never touched. += adds the old row[c] (from above) to the new row[c − 1] (from the left); = would lose the path from above. The answer is the last cell of the row, row[n − 1].
cards/9/q: What is true about Unique Paths and its variations? Select all.
cards/9/options/0: With obstacles it is enough to set dp = 0 in a rock cell — nothing else changes
cards/9/options/1: The formula C(m + n − 2, m − 1) also works with obstacles if you subtract the rocks
cards/9/options/2: In the one-dimensional version row[c] before the update is the value from above, and row[c − 1] is already from the left
cards/9/options/3: Cells can be filled in any order — the transition doesn’t depend on it
cards/9/options/4: Recursion without memoization won’t finish in reasonable time on a 100 × 100 grid
cards/9/explain: A rock is a cell with zero paths into it, and the transition carries that zero onward by itself. The formula counts all paths with no exceptions: a rock removes not one cell but every path through it, and you can’t “just subtract” those. The order must make sure above and left are computed first — that is the fourth DP question. Recursion without memory repeats subproblems, and it makes as many calls as there are paths — up to 10⁵⁸.
cards/10/title: Variations and where this shows up in games
cards/10/body:
Moves from a set {1, 2, 3} or any list: the transition is a sum over all moves, ways[i] = Σ ways[i − s]. That is already the coin problem — the next lesson.

Min Cost Climbing Stairs (#746): every step has a price, the minimum is needed. The transition is the same, but instead of a sum — cost[i] + min(dp[i − 1], dp[i − 2]). “How many ways” turns into “minimum” — only the operation changes.

House Robber (#198): you can’t take two adjacent houses, the sum must be maximal. dp[i] = max(dp[i − 1], dp[i − 2] + a[i]): house i is either skipped or taken together with the best up to i − 2. Two variables as well.

In a game: a table over a grid — when movement across it is simple (only forward and sideways: a runner, a conveyor, a row of tiles) and you need the minimum cost or the number of options. For an arbitrary path across a map that is pathfinding — Dijkstra and A* from the pathfinding unit. And in any per-frame code — a table or variables, not recursion with memo: no stack, no dictionary, zero allocations.
cards/10/deep:
Top-down or bottom-up. Memoization computes only the states the recursion actually reached — a win when there are many states but few are needed (for example, in turn-based games where most positions are unreachable). A table computes everything, but without recursion, without checks and with predictable memory access — on dense problems it is several times faster. In an interview it is fine to start with memoization (it follows directly from the recursion) and then say: “the order is known — I rewrite it as a table, and fold the table into two variables”.

Overflow. Climb(45) = 1 836 311 903 is the last value that fits in an int: Climb(46) = 2 971 215 073 > int.MaxValue. A long holds it up to n = 91. Beyond that — System.Numerics.BigInteger or the answer modulo 10⁹ + 7, as counting problems often ask.

O(log n). The transition is linear: the pair (cur, prev) is multiplied by the matrix [[1, 1], [1, 0]]. So ways[n] is an element of the n-th power of that matrix, and the power is computed by fast exponentiation in O(log n) 2 × 2 multiplications. That is the answer to “faster than O(n)?” — for DP with a linear transition and a huge n (10¹⁸ modulo something).

Combinatorics without overflow. In the Unique Paths formula the intermediate res * (total − k + i) reaches 2·10⁹ · 200, hence long. The division is exact at every step: after i steps res equals C(total − k + i, i) — an integer.

.NET and Unity. int[,] is convenient, but every access checks two bounds; in hot code keep the row in a one-dimensional int[] or Span<int> (for a small row — stackalloc). Array.Fill exists in .NET Core 2.0+ and .NET Standard 2.1 — in Unity since 2021.2; on the old profile — a plain loop.
cards/11/q: You are solving Climbing Stairs out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: only moves of 1 and 2? what is n? is the answer needed modulo something?
cards/11/items/1: Recursion on the last move: ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2)
cards/11/items/2: Its cost: subproblems repeat, there are exponentially many calls
cards/11/items/3: The five questions: state, transition, base, order, answer
cards/11/items/4: A bottom-up table, then two variables: O(n) and O(1)
cards/11/items/6: Edge cases: n = 1, int overflow for n > 45
cards/11/explain: The recursion comes first — it explains where the transition comes from. Its cost explains why DP is needed. The five questions are the frame that shows the interviewer you are building the solution, not recalling it. The run on n = 4 checks the base as well.
cards/12/q: Match each problem with its transition.
